items.title: William Russell Interview, 1976-02-16
items.q: I met him first a couple of times, maybe three times in Washington. And then the last time I saw him was in New York in September of 1939.

ctx.x: Did he then go up to New York again? Is that where you met him?

I met him first a couple of times, maybe three times in Washington. And then the last time I saw him was in New York in September of 1939. Or no, wait, 1940. A couple of months before he went to California. He died out there then six months later. But he did make those... I think the Library of Congress is mostly done in the month of May, probably. They don't have all the dates in the Lomax book, anything about it, exact dates usually. But I don't even know how many it was, but it ran on for several days.
Well, if I'm not mistaken, it was Jelly's music that first got you interested in jazz. And you collected, started collecting.

items.title: William Russell Interview, 1962-09-04
items.q: And the last time I saw jelly was up after I'd been to California a year or so. He came back and a friend of mine took me up to jelly.

ctx.x: He received you very ambly, though.

Yeah, very friendly. When Jelly, you see, there was that seniority business, too, that he wouldn't have, Judy, being younger, wouldn't have dared be leader. Once they wanted Jelly to record with Victor, I mean, with Decca, with Louis Armstrong, is what I'm trying to say, when they made that new Arlene's album that Louis made, and Steve Smith also organized that date. The same one that Judy was in, had a band, and the one where they makes the 219 blues. Sidney Bechet was on the date, too. And Jelly was supposed to…
Which place is that now? Music Box. The same place here.

items.title: William Russell Interview, 1962-08-31
items.q: Are you going to talk about your personal contact with Jelly?

ctx.x: And then also, not that I was just trying to pick Jelly's favorite musicians, but Roy Palmer, whom Jelly also considered the best trombonist. Who had only recorded one very early date with Jelly on an old autograph session. But I had a good interview with him. And also Natty Dominick, who maybe wasn't one of the two or three greatest all-time trumpet players, but certainly had a wonderful rhythmic driving style. One of the choice men as far as personally a wonderful fellow.
Are you going to talk about your personal contact with Jelly?

Yes, I might say, let me finish up first about the notes for jazz men in general. We, one thing I did was to go to the Chicago Defender, the Negro newspaper on the south side, and went through their old files from 1917 on. And I only worked there a couple of days. And I had very sketchy notes, which I wish had been much fuller, because they destroyed those files up to 1923 later. And they began with 1923 to put them on microfilm, which are still available.
